articleTitle: Harmonic sources and filtering approaches
abstract: Traditionally, nonlinear loads have been represented as current sources because their current waveforms are distorted from pure sine-waves at fundamental frequency [l]-[8], A typical harmonic source is a phase-controlled thyristor rectifier having a sufficient dc inductance to produce a nonpulsating dc current. Accordingly, parallel, or shunt, passive and parallel-active filters are commonly applied to nonlinear loads to mitigate harmonics. The principle of the parallel-passive filter is to provide a low-impedance shunt branch to the load's harmonic current, thus reducing harmonic current flowing into the source. The principle of the parallel-active filter is to inject harmonic current with the same amplitude and opposite phase of the load's harmonic current into the line, thus eliminating harmonic current flowing into the source. Indeed, the parallel-passive and -active filters are effective for compensating such current-source nonlinear loads [9]-[20].

articleTitle: A battery management system for stand-alone photovoltaic energy systems
abstract: It is estimated that about 80% of all photovoltaic (PV) modules are used in stand-alone applications [1]. Continuous power is obtained from PV systems by using a storage buffer, typically in the form of a lead acid battery.

articleTitle: Ambient-proportional sensing control reduces heat tracing costs
abstract: The majority of heat tracing applications deal with winterization for water and water-based processes. Whether for piping, tanks, or instruments, control of freeze protection systems are often simple, but not energy efficient. The following approach to this basic application has yielded direct benefits to users through an alternative control method that typically uses a single-pole thermostat to switch a multipole contactor installed between the main circuit breaker and a distribution panel board that energizes multiple heating circuits. This provides control with minimal cost in design and installation (Fig. 1).

articleTitle: Coupling rectifier systems with harmonic cancelling reactors
abstract: The widespread use of power electronic equipment has given rise to the serious harmonic pollution of power lines. Transformer-coupled double rectifier systems, so-called 12-phase rectifier systems, are widely used as a simple utility interface with improved current waveforms for mid- and high-power applications [1], [2]. However, they require line-frequency input transformers which make the devices bulky and expensive. This has driven the development of economical rectifier systems with high efficiencies and low costs.

articleTitle: The impact of the induction motor on short-circuit current
abstract: Simplified analytical models for calculation of the induction motor's short-circuit current are being presented. Laboratory tests have been performed on two induction motors with low power rating, 26 kW and 122 kW, respectively, in order to measure their short-circuit current. Results calculated according to the available literature have been compared to those acquired by testing. Calculations have also been made for a high-voltage induction motor rated 1250 kW, whose parameters have, been known.

articleTitle: Industrial speed control: are PM couplings an alternative to VFDs?
abstract: Recent surveys indicate that fans/blowers and pumps comprise between 40% and 50% of all industrial loads (rated by energy consumption), which accounts for several hundred billion kilowatthours in the United States annually. It is important to perform these most fundamental of industrial functions as efficiently as possible; however, the traditional means of regulating the flow from these loads, by throttling valves for pumps and baffling vanes for fans, are well known to be inefficient. The wasted energy is dissipated as heat in the throttling systems themselves, as well as in the fluids being circulated in the industrial processes.

articleTitle: Simple control for a wind-driven induction generator
abstract: Global environmental concerns and the ever-increasing need for energy spur the search for new opportunities to use renewable energy sources. Harnessing electrical energy from wind power is a cost-effective and cleaner option. The generated power can be fed directly into the grid or used to feed the local loads. The self-excited induction generators are becoming popular with the proliferation of such nonconventional energy sources as wind, small hydro projects, etc. The induction generators (particularly squirrel-cage induction generators) have robust construction, lower initial and run-time cost (due to brushless construction), and lower maintenance cost [1], The induction generators are suitable for grid-connected as well as standalone applications. In grid-connected mode, the excitation current to the induction generator is supplied through the grid. A mechanical arrangement is used to maintain the rotor speed above the synchronous speed. In self-excitation mode, the excitation current is supplied by a local source.

articleTitle: High-resistance ground retrofits in pulp and paper mills
abstract: The safety and reliability of low-voltage, high-resistance grounding schemes have made them an excellent choice for applications in the pulp, paper, and other process industries. As facilities shift toward this technology for reliability in low-voltage substations, retrofitting existing grounded systems becomes the focus of several critical application considerations. This article will briefly review different grounding methods and their theories of operation. Then, examples of actual installations will be presented that will identify potential misapplications of high-resistance ground retrofits, discuss typical ground voltages and currents, and present important considerations for reliable and safe installation of HRG equipment.

articleTitle: Excitation control of the synchronous generator
abstract: In a world of change, new technologies replace old ones ever-more quickly. In the early years, change was slow as the evolutionary process transitioned from electromechanical voltage regulators with motor-driven rheostats to high-gain rotating exciters. These exciters included such systems as the Amplidyne, Regulex, and Rototrol, which improved performance to control the generator output. In the past 30 years, however, change has progressed from magnetic technology to analog control. Analog excitation represented the multiple component module assembly with interlooping wire interconnections (see Fig. 1).

articleTitle: Networked intelligent motor-control systems
abstract: The integration of intelligent devices, device-level networks, and software into motor-control systems can deliver improved diagnostics, early warnings for increased system reliability, design flexibility, and simplified wiring. Remote access to motor-control information also affords an opportunity for reduced exposure to hazardous voltages and improved personnel safety during startup and troubleshooting. This article explores the communication-cable requirements, intelligent devices, and software required to integrate these new technologies into motor-control systems. It also reviews the issues, changes in thinking, and advantages that were found during the installation and startup of a plant system.

articleTitle: Drive systems for high-speed gearless elevators
abstract: The advent of modem high-rise buildings has brought about the need for highspeed lift systems to provide quick access within these buildings {1}. The general structure of high-speed lift systems is shown in Fig. 1. The dynamic arrangement of the complete system can be divided into three sections; they can be thought of separately, but are dynamically coupled. First, there is the electrical drive system which includes closed-loop control of the velocity of the main sheave. The second part comprises the ropes and the various masses with which they interconnect, the characteristics of which are dependent upon the position of the lift in the shaft. Finally, there is the set of isolation pads which joins the car to the sling.

articleTitle: Managing aviation safety through inspection information technology
abstract: According to Boeing estimates, as of the year 2000, more than half of the aircarrier fleet worldwide was flying out-of-production aircraft. Many of these aircraft are operating beyond their model design service objectives (DSOs) and for a second or third operator. Some newer commercial aircraft have had their DSO extended from 20 to 30 years; the DSOs for some military aircraft have been extended 40 to 65 years. Of all the commercial aircraft flying today, approximately 20% are in the aging aircraft category. As this number increases, so does the need for heightened fleet monitoring by the operators, the manufacturers, and the regulatory agencies [1].

articleTitle: Five-level double converters for induction motor drives
abstract: In recent years, multilevel power converters for high power applications have been actively investigated [l]-[5]. In particular, three-level drive systems have been put to practical uses. Applying such converters to large motor drive systems makes it possible to omit transformers, which have drawbacks such as installation space and cost. However, multilevel power converters have certain disadvantages, such as the need to balance the voltage of the dc-bus capacitors. In five-level inverters fed to ac drives, it is difficult to maintain the five-level dc voltages as they tend to rise or fall monotonously. Hence, we have proposed a pulsewidth modulation (PWM) control method for a five-level rectifier used as a dc power source for the five-level inverter [6]. This method is able to maintain the output dc-bus capacitor voltages, keep the input power factor at near unity, and regenerate electric power back to the power system.

articleTitle: Formation of ceramic thin films using electrospray in cone-jet mode
abstract: Over the past two decades, there has been a significant growth of interest in research and development in the advanced ceramic industry. The advanced ceramic industry covers a wide and diverse range of products of which ceramic films and coatings are one of the most important applications, especially in electrical, electronic, electromechanical, and thermal industries in order to solve many corrosion, electrical insulation, wear, and thermal protection problems.

articleTitle: Short-circuit, coordination, and harmonic studies
abstract: According to the IEEE Brown Book (ANSI/IEEE Standard 399-1990), “The planning, design and operation of a power system requires continual and comprehensive analyses to evaluate current system performance and to establish the effectiveness of alternative plans for system expansion.”

articleTitle: Digital excitation enhances performance and improves diagnostics
abstract: New digital excitation systems are being introduced that provide many advantages over existing systems. Chief among these improvements are advances in performance and diagnostics. In addition to the classic excitation functions, new features provide additional protection. One innovation that has been added to some of the previous limiter functions modifies the pickup point based on external conditions. Additionally, entirely new limiter functions and monitoring capabilities have been added. These enhancements allow the generator to operate closer to its design limit and help keep the unit online during adverse conditions, increasing reliability and reducing down time.

articleTitle: Partnerships for electrical safety
abstract: In the increasing complexity of the global marketplace, employees are expected to integrate electrical safety practices into the continuous workplace transitions that competition and innovation bring. Essentially workers are challenged to distinguish between acceptable risks in doing jobs, interacting with technologies, and adapting to different environments, and unacceptable risks, like performing electrical maintenance tasks hurriedly or avoiding the inconvenience of personal protective gear.

articleTitle: North American and IEC standards for circuit breakers
abstract: Which standards are appropriate for molded-case circuit breakers in North America—North American or International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) standards? It seems a strange question to ask until we recognize that various entities are wondering whether IEC standards are appropriate to apply to products in North America. Multinational organizations may wish to use one electrical system worldwide, including interchangeable components. Then again, some countries may not want the burden of maintaining a country standard. Since IEC stands for “International Electrotechnical Commission,” its name implies international usage. Though IEC standards are generally international, they are not adopted worldwide. In contrast, it is not always recognized that the National Electrical Code (NEC or code) is also international [1], Although the NEC is the installation code for the United States, versions of the NEC are used in Mexico, the Philippines, Panama, Costa Rica, Venezuela, and Puerto Rico and are being considered elsewhere. The installation code for Canada is in close correlation with the NEC. Further, the product standards for molded-case circuit breakers in the three North American countries are largely identical to each other, but not equivalent to the IEC standards for circuit breakers. These product standards could also be considered international, at least in content.

articleTitle: Designing industrial systems with a weak utility supply
abstract: The quality of power available for industrial customers is almost always an important concern in site evaluations for new facilities. In many situations, sag and outage rates, voltage distortion, and other factors are provided by the local utility company. The industrial power engineer, therefore, is concerned with evaluating the effects of various supply system anomalies on the process equipment within the plant.

articleTitle: Which project-execution approach is best for you?
abstract: In recent years, substantial growth in the economies of the Americas has resulted in a record number of capital projects I that have been announced or are in different stages of execution in the cement industry in this region [1]. In the United States, for example, with, the passage of the Transportation Equity Act for the 21st Century (TEA 21), it is I expected that highway and bridge construction will rise considerably in the years to come [2], triggering further developments in cement projects.

articleTitle: Reduce raptor mortality by retrofitting power lines
abstract: Moon Lake Electric Association (MLEA) was sentenced to three years probation on 12 August 1999 for electrocuting 17 eagles and hawks near Rangely, CO. The utility pled guilty to six violations of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act and the Eagle Protection Act. Under the settlement, MLEA agreed to pay a $50,000 fine, donate $50,000 to further raptor conservation, and enter into a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS). The MOU clarified utility obligations to protect birds and required a plan to prevent future bird deaths.

articleTitle: Reliability program for plant maintenance
abstract: With the increased emphasis on cost containment and reduction, the reliability of equipment has become an area of great concern. Many managers now see reliability-centered maintenance (RCM) as a method of gaining an advantage over the competition. What does reliability entail, and how can a RCM process be implemented? This article defines what a reliability process involves and illustrates how a reliability process was implemented at the Catawba, SC, site of the Bowater Coated Paper Division. Both the successes and the growing pains experienced will be discussed with thoughts on how the implementation could have gone smoother. The greatest benefits gained from the process will be mentioned and plans for where to carry the process in the future will be explored.

articleTitle: Applying CTs with digital ground relays
abstract: Industrial power-distribution-system substation transformers and generator step-up transformers in power stations (Fig. 1 shown above) often use resistance-grounded wye secondary windings for medium-voltage power distribution. The purpose of this is to limit damage due to ground-fault currents, while providing sufficient fault current for the operation of ground-fault relaying. The relaying used to protect against ground faults in the system may not provide sufficient protection of the transformer winding against internal faults because the backup ground overcurrent relay in the transformer neutral-to-ground connection must be set to coordinate with downstream relays. In order to protect the winding itself, special relays are utilized [1].

articleTitle: Electrical safety activities and opportunities in the power systems engineering committee
abstract: The Power Systems Engineering Committee of the Industrial and Commercial Power Systems (I&CPS) Department has long provided a focal point for electrical safety in the IAS. Its scope spans the design, analysis, installation, grounding, operation, and maintenance of safe and reliable power systems, including emergency and standby systems for industrial, commercial, and institutional facilities. The committee, its subcommittees, and working groups meet twice a year at the I&CPS Technical Conference in May and the IAS Annual Meeting in the fall. If you are interested in becoming involved in the professional and technical development opportunities offered by the Power Systems Engineering Committee, e-mail one of the Committee officers or key contacts: □ Chair Lynn Saunders lynn.saunders@ieee.org □ Vice Chair Mark Halpin halpin@ece.msstate.edu □ Secretary Matt Dozier mdozier@idesignservices.com.

articleTitle: The nuts and bolts of a good installation
abstract: Most oil exploration and subsequent refining operations take place outside the continental areas of North America and Europe. There, the National Electrical Code (NEC), Canadian Electrical Code (CEC), and CENELEC standards are not the de facto codes and standards to which firms must adhere.

articleTitle: Lockout energy control placarding for power distribution equipment
abstract: The use of lockout techniques is required in most facilities, including power distribution facilities, but is often established in many different ways. Often times flags, tags, the instructions of a system operator, or other means are utilized in power distribution facilities to approximate the same level of safety as is afforded by use of actual physical locks. Extensive training is required to maintain the integrity of these alternate systems, but the chance of error is greater than in the systems where locks are used. Use of personal locks also squarely places the responsibility of achieving the electrically safe condition of the equipment upon the worker or employee.

articleTitle: Current signature analysis to detect induction motor faults
abstract: Three-phase induction motors are the “workhorses” of industry and are the most widely used electrical machines. In an industrialized nation, they can typically consume between 40 to 50% of all the generated capacity of that country. This article focuses on the industrial application of motor current signature analysis (MCSA) to diagnose faults in three-phase induction motor drives. MCSA is a noninvasive, on-line monitoring technique for the diagnosis of problems in induction motors. Reliability-based maintenance (RBM) and condition-based maintenance (CBM) strategies are now widely used by industry, and health monitoring of electrical drives is a major feature in such programs.

articleTitle: Planning for distributed generation
abstract: Utility distribution system planners strive to determine optimal expansion strategies to provide reliable, economical service. Typically, distribution planners project the load growth for several years and then estimate when a capacity limit will be exceeded at some peak loading condition. They often assume the failure of one key circuit element, such as a substation transformer or a main feeder. Some planners may design for two failures. When this analysis predicts that the voltage will be too low or that the current in a line or substation transformer will be too high, investment in new capacity is mandated. However, investment options are usually restricted to substation or feeder expansion. Planners then consider a few feasible alternatives for solving the problem and select the one that best meets their performance and cost objectives.

articleTitle: Arcing fault hazards and safety suggestions for design and maintenance
abstract: In recent years, significant progress has been made in understanding the hazards of arcing faults to maintenance personnel working on electrical equipment. The National Electrical Code (NEC) requires that equipment be installed the way it is listed and labeled. However, the NEC and product standards do not address the hazards associated when the equipment doors are open and a maintenance worker accidentally creates an arcing fault.

articleTitle: A different kind of chemistry: a history of tungsten halogen lamps
abstract: The 1992 Energy Policy Act (EPACT) brought significant changes to the U.S. electric-lighting industry. One such change required replacing many ordinary incandescent lamps with more energy-efficient tungsten halogen lamps. Tungsten halogen, though, is by no means a new development. As we near the golden anniversary of the halogen lamp's invention, it seems appropriate to look back and explore the roots of the most important extension of incandescent lighting technology since 1913.

articleTitle: Ground systems design considerations for vessels [in petroleum industry]
abstract: Tanks and vessels have numerous grounded and protection systems. These include static discharge from fluid-movement bonding, lightning-protection ground, lightning-discharge halo, equipment bonding, cathodic protection, stray-current control, power and external-line protection, instrumentation connection, and instrumentation protection.

articleTitle: Choosing electric turbocompressor drivers
abstract: The Dutch NAM, a joint venture of Esso and Shell, as the owner and operator of the giant Groningen gas field in the north of The Netherlands, is the largest producer of natural gas in the Netherlands. After 35 years of production, the reservoir pressure of this field has declined, and three underground gas storage (UGS) reservoirs were installed to cope with peak demand. This article reports on the injection compressor drivers.

articleTitle: NFPA 70E 2000: updating electrical safety requirements for employee workplaces
abstract: The Williams-Steiger Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSH Act) of 1970 was passed by the Congress of the United States of America (USA) to assure safe and healthful working conditions for working men and women. The Act became effective on April 28, 1971. The initial policy of the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), regarding electrical safety requirements, was to incorporate into the Act, by reference, the various national consensus standards such as the National Fire Protection Association's (NFPA) 1968 National Electrical Code(NEC). On March 15, 1972, an amendment to the regulations adopted the 1971 NEC. As time advanced, the U.S. courts established chat compliance with the NEC resulted in installations having provisions considered necessary for safety. However, the NEC lacked safety standards for work practices. By 1975, OSHA encouraged NFPA to undertake the cask of condensing the portions of the NEC covering chose elements directly associated with personnel safety into a document chat could be used as a guide for inspection of employee work places. On January 7, 1976, the NFPA 70E Committee was activated, functioning under the National Electrical Code Correlating Committee. The NFPA 70E Committee was formed to assist OSHA in preparing electrical safety standards that would serve OSHA's needs. Their charter was to produce a document chat addressed personnel-related safety issues, which could be used as a guide for inspection of employee work places. NFP A 70E had to be capable of crossing two major hurdles: one being the standard NFPA consensus development process, and the other being the recognition process required under the Occupational Safety and Health Acc.

articleTitle: Proper grounding of on-site electrical power systems
abstract: For optimum personnel safety, equipment protection, and power continuity to electrical loads, proper on-site power system grounding is essential. If the on-site power is the sole source of power, then its grounding is relatively straightforward and follows the National Electrical Code (NEC) Article 250. However, if the on-site power system serves an alternate source of power (i.e., emergency or standby power), then the grounding becomes more complex. Furthermore, portable and mobile generators have special grounding requirements.

articleTitle: Cold-weather effects on Class I hazardous electrical installations
abstract: With electrical hazardous area installations in different climates around the world, it is increasingly difficult to test products for all temperature extremes. When standard testing for Class I explosion-proof equipment generally covers the temperature range of +40 to —25 °C (104 to —13 °F), how do you design for climates which may encounter much lower temperatures? In cold climate areas such as Alaska, Northern Canada, and Siberia, temperatures as low as −50 to −70 °C (−58 to —94 °F) may be encountered.

articleTitle: Toward alignment of safety levels concerning electrical installations in the EU
abstract: The European Standard EN 50110-1 “Operation of Electrical Installations” [1] is applicable to all operation of and work activity on, with, or near electrical installations. These installations operate at voltage levels from and including extra-low voltage up to and including high voltage (medium and extra-high voltage), and they are designed for the generation, transmission, conversion, distribution and use of electrical power. Some of these electrical installations are permanent and fixed, such as a distribution installation in a factory or office complex.

articleTitle: Optimizing capital costs in power-distribution upgrades
abstract: The existing North American inventory of paper mills is older and less efficient than their counterparts in emerging markets, such as Asia and South America. Over the past several years, North American paper companies have kept pace by adding new capacity using current technologies to compete in world markets. Capacity expansion will likely result in a need to review interrupting ratings for existing equipment in order to assure that the electrical distribution system is able to support the additional source mega-voltamperes (MVA).

articleTitle: North American zones: rethinking hazardous location design
abstract: Recent changes to the Canadian Electrical Code (CEC) (1998) and National Electrical Code (NEC) (1996 and 1998), while progressive, are only first steps. The updates allow the use of the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) classification system and products. For the purposes of this article, the CEC is used as a starting point.

articleTitle: The global HazLoc impact of the IECEx scheme
abstract: The IECEx Scheme is an international certification scheme intended to facilitate global trade in electrical equipment for use in hazardous (classified) locations. Such hazardous locations are also commonly referred to as explosive atmospheres, with the equipment for use in such locations or atmospheres commonly referred to as HazLoc equipment or Ex equipment. The scheme provides a structured system to achieve global acceptance for explosion-protected equipment designed for hazardous locations. Scheme members declare that they will abolish national differences for product requirements in their countries during the coming years. This international scheme will greatly impact the free trade of explosion-protected apparatus needed for the petrochemical and chemical industry if the scheme members recognize and accept harmonized worldwide International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) standards. The goal is to develop and maintain uniform product evaluation to protect users against products that are not compliant with the required level of safety.

articleTitle: Reducing the effects of lightning in cogeneration plants
abstract: Georgia Transmission Corporation (GTC), an electric utility company, serves the Weyerhaeuser Flint River Mill in Oglethorpe, GA, with a new, nondedicated 115 kV radial-transmission line connecting from the North Americus substation with a tap to the South Oglethorpe substation. The Flint River mill is a cogenerator with a single 46.6 MVA steam-turbine generator fueled by biomass.

articleTitle: Comparing US and international power and control cable standards
abstract: From the engineer’s perspective, the specification, selection, testing, application, and installation of wire and cable is becoming more complicated as we move further into the age of the “global economy.” No longer can engineering firms in their respective countries rely on their domestic standards for the application and installation of wire and cable on export or offshore projects. It is now necessary for cable engineers to have a working knowledge of international standards so they can specify the proper cable for installation across the globe. Herein lies the difficulty that most of the cable engineers face—the unfamiliarity with international standards.

articleTitle: David C. Prince-engineer, researcher, inventor
abstract: David Chandler Prince influenced electrical switchgear design in a way paralleled by few other engineers. He made decisions and took actions that changed forever the way power engineers design and apply switchgear. His contributions continue to influence this work. Prior to 1925, switching technologies were mostly an empirical art based on hydraulic conceptions of arc interruption. By 1935, art evolved into science based on an electronic or plasma view of electric arc behavior. Prince led the way as engineers worldwide extended switchgear technologies from bulk oil and air magnetic to new frontiers of vacuum, minimum oil, oil blast, and air blast. In addition, he wrote one of the first textbooks on mercury-arc rectifiers and coined the term “inverter,” so commonly used today.

articleTitle: Update: offshore electrical installation practices
abstract: The offshore industry had its beginning in 1947, when the first offshore platform was installed off the coast of Louisiana in 25 ft of water. There was very little need for electrical systems then and, when used, they consisted of a battery supply for the aids-to-navigation systems and small portable generating plants for localized lighting of nighttime drilling activities. As the search for oil and gas progressed, platforms were located further offshore in deeper waters. This necessitated the requirement for offshore living quarters located on the platforms because the time lost to commuting grew to undesirable levels. Thus, the generation of electricity became a natural part of the scene on most platforms as the requirements grew to include cooking, heating and air conditioning, and lighting requirements for living quarters.

articleTitle: A survey of rural utility safety issues and practices
abstract: There exists an old cliché that reads, "An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure,” a very true statement for utility operations. It's reported that utilities incur millions of dollars in costs annually, most of which are covered by insurance, as a result of accidents. This includes lost time productivity of injured employees, higher insurance rates, and higher workman compensation rates. The National Safety Council (NSC) Injury Facts 1998 data indicates there were 4.72 incident rates per 100 employees for the electric services industry. From that number, there were 2.47 workers per 100 employees who experienced a lost work day as the result of an accident. The average number of lost work days per injured employee reported in this publication was 57.

articleTitle: The industry applications society under the IEEE umbrella
abstract: The Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers (IEEE) had its beginning over 116 years ago, when Dr. Nathaniel Keith called a meeting of a group of electrical inventors and entrepreneurs on 13 May 1884, in New York City, to form the “American Institute of Electrical Engineers (AIEE),” and elected Norvin Green its first President. Their mission as stated was “To promote the arts and sciences of ELECTRICITY.” They held their first regular meeting in Philadelphia on 7-8 October 1884.

articleTitle: Joseph Slepian, Part II - 1947 IEEE Edison medallist
abstract: In the November/December 2000 issne of IEEE Industry Applications Magazine, we profiled mathematician, scientist, engineer, and inventor Joseph Slepian. His career was so impressive that he was awarded the AIEE Edison Medal in 1947, “for his theoretical and practical contributions to power systems through circuit analysis, arc control, and current interruption.”

articleTitle: Volume VII index
abstract: This index covers all technical items — papers, correspondence, reviews, etc. that appeared in this periodical during 2001, and items from previous years that were commented upon or corrected in 2001. Departments and other items may be also covered if they have been judged to have archival value.

articleTitle: The IEEE brown book [Book Review]
abstract: This column is devoted to a discussion of the IEEE Brown Book. Officially, the IEEE Brown Book is IEEE Standard 399, Recommended Practice for Industrial and Commercial Power Systems Analysis, and it was last revised in 1997. The IEEE Brown Book is now being revised under the leadership of Guy Jackson (gjackson@powerplot.com). If you are interested in participating in the development of the revised IEEE Brown Book, feel free to contact Chairperson Jackson or, better yet, attend either the IAS Industrial and Commercial Power Systems conference (held each May) or the IAS Annual Meeting (held each October) and participate in person.

articleTitle: The ieee green book
abstract: This column is devoted to a discussion of the IEEE Green Book. Officially, the IEEE Green Book is IEEE Standard 142, Recommended Practice for Grounding of Industrial And Commercial Power Systems, and it was last revised in 1991. At this time, the IEEE Green Book is completing a revision under the leadership of Lynn Saunders (lynn.saunders@ieee.org). If you would like to participate in the development of the next revision, contact Chairperson Saunders or, better yet, attend either the IEEE IAS Industrial and Commercial Power Systems Conference or the IEEE IAS Annual Meeting and get involved and participate in person. (Both meetings are listed in our 2001 Conference Calendar here in the magazine and at the website www.ieee.org/ias.)

articleTitle: Color books
abstract: I his column is devoted to a discussion of the IEEE Orange Book. Officially, the IEEE Orange Book is IEEE Standard 446, Recommended Practice for Emergency and Standby Power Systems for Industrial and Commercial Applications. The IEEE Orange Book has just been reaffirmed under the leadership of Charles Hughes (cdhughes@ieee.org). The next chairperson, Jim Daley (jdaley@asco.com), has already been selected to lead the next five years of work in this important area. If you are interested in participating in the development of the next revision of the IEEE Orange Book, feel free to contact Chairperson Daley or, better yet, attend either the IAS Industrial and Commercial Power Systems Conference (held each May) or the IAS Annual Meeting (held each October) and get involved and participate in person.
